content: Glucocorticoids are the cornerstone of treatment for croup in children. Existing research has consistently demonstrated their efficacy in managing this condition. However, it is essential to continually update the evidence to ensure their clinical relevance remains well-supported. This review represents an update to prior reviews published in 1999, 2004, 2011, and 2018. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects and safety of glucocorticoids in children aged 18 years or younger who were diagnosed with croup. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared glucocorticoids to placebo, other pharmacologic agents, different glucocorticoids, or varying doses and modes of administration. The studies needed to assess at least one primary outcome, such as changes in croup scores or hospital readmissions, or secondary outcomes, such as length of hospital stay, patient improvement, use of additional treatments, or adverse events. The search for relevant studies was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Library, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, WHO ICTRP, and ClinicalTrials.gov, with the most recent search performed on March 4, 2022. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by multiple reviewers, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. This updated review included 45 RCTs involving a total of 5,888 children, which represents an increase of two RCTs and 1,323 children since the last update. One ongoing study and one study awaiting classification were also identified. Most of the included studies (98%) were assessed as having a high or unclear risk of bias. When comparing glucocorticoids to placebo, the evidence suggests that glucocorticoids may lead to greater reductions in croup scores at two hours (low-certainty evidence), six hours (low-certainty evidence), and 12 hours (low-certainty evidence) after treatment. However, the evidence for changes in croup scores at 24 hours was very uncertain (very low-certainty evidence). When comparing one glucocorticoid to another, there was little to no difference between prednisolone and dexamethasone in reducing croup scores at two hours (high-certainty evidence) or six hours (moderate-certainty evidence) post-treatment. However, dexamethasone likely reduced the rate of return visits or hospital readmissions for croup by nearly half (moderate-certainty evidence) and decreased the need for additional glucocorticoid treatments by 28% (moderate-certainty evidence). When comparing different doses of dexamethasone, a higher dose of 0.60 mg/kg likely reduced croup severity at 24 hours compared to a lower dose of 0.15 mg/kg (moderate-certainty evidence). However, there was no significant difference in croup severity at two hours (high-certainty evidence) or six hours (moderate-certainty evidence), and the evidence at 12 hours was very uncertain (very low-certainty evidence). There was little to no difference between doses in terms of return visits or hospital readmissions (high-certainty evidence), length of hospital stay, or the need for additional treatments such as epinephrine, intubation, or supplemental glucocorticoids. Adverse events were reported in some of the comparisons, but the review did not provide detailed conclusions regarding their frequency or severity. In conclusion, the evidence supporting the use of glucocorticoids to reduce croup symptoms, shorten hospital stays, and decrease return visits or readmissions remains consistent with previous findings. A lower dose of dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg) may be as effective as the standard dose (0.60 mg/kg), but further RCTs are needed to confirm the efficacy of low-dose dexamethasone in treating croup.
